<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-kernel}
There is a surjective root-degree map from the spectral monomial lattice to
\(\mathsf L\), with kernel generated by the root monomials, such that
\begin{equation}\label{eq:intro-kernel}
 2D^{(2)}(m,n)-D_0(m,n)=\omega_Q(\deg_Qm,\deg_Qn).
\end{equation}
Consequently, after adjoining \(w\) with \(w^2=u\), the toroidal product is
the graded twist of the one-parameter product at \(v=t_0u\) given by
\[
 x*y=w^{\omega_Q(\alpha,\beta)}(x*_v y)
 \qquad(\deg_Qx=\alpha,\ \deg_Qy=\beta).
\]
The same statement holds for the subalgebras generated by the truncated
fundamental characters of \(\mathscr C_Q\).
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:intro-main}
For every connected bipartite Dynkin quiver of type
\(A_n,D_n,E_6,E_7\), or \(E_8\), the assignment \(E_i\mapsto Z_i\) induces
an isomorphism
\[
 U_{\mathbf q}^{+}(\mathfrak g)\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\
 \mathcal G_R(Q)\otimes_RK.
\]
For each source--sink edge \(r\to s\), the local conjugation spectrum is
\[
\operatorname{Spec}_{Z_r}(Z_s)=\{t_0t,t_0^{-1}\}.
\]
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:lower}
Each monomial in \(F_\infty(m_+)\), and in its specialization or
truncation, has the form \(m_+\prod A_{i,r}^{-v_{i,r}}\) with
\(v_{i,r}\in\mathbb Z_{\geq0}\) of finite support. The analogous assertion holds for
\(F_v(m_+)\).
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
In the recursive construction, an \(i\)-expansion at a monomial \(m\)
is assembled from factors \eqref{eq:screening-generator}. Each term has
exponent vector equal to that of \(m\) minus a nonnegative sum of
\(a_{i,r}\). Ordered products change only scalar coefficients. Thus the
cone \(m_+\prod A_{i,r}^{-\mathbb Z_{\geq0}}\) is stable under every expansion at a
monomial already in the cone. The correction steps take linear combinations
of such expansions and cannot introduce a new exponent vector outside it.
Induction over the finite sequence of steps producing a given term proves
the assertion for the recursive construction of \cite[Theorem 5.8]{FH}.
Specialization may cancel terms, and truncation deletes terms; neither
operation creates an exponent vector. The one-parameter proof is identical.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:telescope}
For \(d=p-s\) one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:D2closed}
 D^{(2)}(Y_{i,p},Y_{j,s})
       =\widetilde C_{ij}(d-1)-\widetilde C_{ij}(-d-1).
\end{equation}
In particular, when \(p>s\), this equals \(\widetilde C_{ij}(p-s-1)\).
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
Abbreviate \(c(m)=\widetilde C_{ij}(m)\). Substitution of \(a=-2h\) into
\eqref{eq:Na} gives
\begin{align*}
 -\sum_{h=1}^{M}N_{-2h}(i,p;j,s)
 ={}&\sum_{h=1}^{M}\bigl(c(d+1-2h)-c(d-1-2h)\bigr)\\
 &+\sum_{h=1}^{M}\bigl(c(-d-1-2h)-c(-d+1-2h)\bigr)\\
 ={}&c(d-1)-c(d-1-2M)\\
 &+c(-d-1-2M)-c(-d-1).
\end{align*}
Choose \(M\) large enough that both terminal arguments are nonpositive.
All subsequent summands vanish, and both terminal coefficients are zero.
This proves \eqref{eq:D2closed}. The argument includes \(d=0\) and
negative \(d\); the formula is visibly skew-symmetric.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:mesh}
The assignment
\[
 e_{i,p}\longmapsto\beta_{i,p}
       =\tau^{(\xi_i-p)/2}\gamma_i
\]
induces an isomorphism of abelian groups
\begin{equation}\label{eq:meshquotient}
 \mathcal P/\mathsf R\ \xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\ \mathsf L.
\end{equation}
Consequently \(\deg_Q\) in \eqref{eq:degree-candidate} is surjective,
\(\ker\deg_Q=\mathsf R\), and \(\deg_Q A_{i,r}=0\).
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Write the coordinates of a root as \((x,y)\), with source coordinates
first, and let \(B\) be the source--sink incidence matrix. The products of
commuting reflections in the two colors act by
\[
 s_+(x,y)=(-x+By,y),\qquad s_-(x,y)=(x,-y+B^Tx).
\]
Thus \(\tau=s_+s_-\). The vectors on the initial slice are
\[
 \gamma_i=(e_i,0)\quad(i\in I_+),\qquad
 \gamma_j=(Be_j,e_j)\quad(j\in I_-).
\]
They are a \(\mathbb Z\)-basis of \(\mathsf L\), since their change-of-basis matrix
is block triangular with identity diagonal blocks. Direct substitution gives
\begin{align}
 \tau\gamma_i+\gamma_i&=\sum_{j\sim i}\gamma_j
                          &&(i\in I_+),\label{eq:meshsource}\\
 \tau^{-1}\gamma_j+\gamma_j&=\sum_{i\sim j}\gamma_i
                          &&(j\in I_-).\label{eq:meshsink}
\end{align}
Their translates by powers of \(\tau\) are precisely
\[
 \beta_{i,r-1}+\beta_{i,r+1}
                  -\sum_{j\sim i}\beta_{j,r}=0.
\]
Hence \(\mathsf R\) lies in the kernel of the proposed map.

In \(\mathcal P/\mathsf R\), the same recurrence expresses every generator in terms
of the slice \(e_{i,1}\) for \(i\in I_+\) and \(e_{j,0}\) for
\(j\in I_-\). For example, moving downward first determines the source
layer at \(-1\) from the layers at \(1,0\), then the sink layer at
\(-2\), and so on. Moving upward first determines the sink layer at
\(2\), then the source layer at \(3\). At each step the coefficient of
the new layer is \(1\); no division is involved. Thus the slice classes
generate the quotient. Their images are the basis \(\{\gamma_i\}\),
so they have no relation. This proves \eqref{eq:meshquotient}.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:Aindependent}
The exponent vectors \(a_{i,r}\) are linearly independent for finite
integer combinations. In particular, a finite expression
\(m=m_+\prod A_{i,r}^{-v_{i,r}}\) has uniquely determined exponents
\(v_{i,r}\).
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Suppose \(\sum c_{i,r}a_{i,r}=0\) is a nonzero finite relation and
choose the largest \(r\) with some \(c_{i,r}\ne0\). The coefficient of
\(e_{i,r+1}\) in the relation is \(c_{i,r}\): any other contributing
root monomial would have center \(r+1\) or \(r+2\), both larger than
the chosen maximum. Hence every \(c_{i,r}\) at the maximal level is
zero, a contradiction.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:local-AY}
For each admissible pair one has
\begin{align}
 D_0(A_{i,r},Y_{j,s})
   &=2\delta_{ij}\bigl(\delta_{r-s,1}-\delta_{s-r,1}\bigr),
           \label{eq:A-D0}\\
 D^{(2)}(A_{i,r},Y_{j,s})
   &=\delta_{ij}\bigl(\delta_{r-s,1}-\delta_{s-r,1}\bigr).
           \label{eq:A-D2}
\end{align}
Thus \(\Omega(a_{i,r},e_{j,s})=0\).
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Put \(c_{ij}(m)=\widetilde C_{ij}(m)\). With the zero extension, the inverse
Cartan recurrence may be written at all integer arguments as
\begin{equation}\label{eq:delta-mesh}
 c_{ij}(m+1)+c_{ij}(m-1)-\sum_{k\sim i}c_{kj}(m)
                  =\delta_{ij}\delta_{m,0}.
\end{equation}
For \(m\ge1\) this is the recurrence, for \(m=0\) it is
\(c_{ij}(1)=\delta_{ij}\), and for \(m<0\) both sides are zero.
Expand the first argument \(A_{i,r}\) in \eqref{eq:D2closed}. The
four root-monomial contributions form \eqref{eq:delta-mesh} at
\(m=r-s-1\) and at \(m=s-r-1\), with opposite signs. The result is
\eqref{eq:A-D2}. Applying the same expansion to \(N_0\) in
\eqref{eq:Na} gives two copies of this boundary difference, proving
\eqref{eq:A-D0}. These formulas also agree with the specialized
\(A\)--\(Y\) relation of \cite[\S7]{FH}; the computation fixes the
ordered-pair signs without an implicit orientation convention.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:kernel}
For all finite Laurent monomials \(m,n\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:kernel-main}
 2D^{(2)}(m,n)-D_0(m,n)=\omega_Q(\deg_Qm,\deg_Qn).
\end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
By \cref{lem:local-AY}, \(\Omega(a_{i,r},e_{j,s})=0\) for every
root-monomial generator and every spectral basis vector. Skew-symmetry
then gives \(\Omega(e_{j,s},a_{i,r})=0\). Hence \(\mathsf R\) lies in the
radical in both variables, so \(\Omega\) descends to a well-defined skew
form on \(\mathcal P/\mathsf R\). By \cref{lem:mesh} this quotient is \(\mathsf L\). It is
therefore enough to compute the descended form on the slice whose images
are \(\gamma_i\). If both vertices belong to the same color,
their slice positions agree, so \(D_0=D^{(2)}=0\). If \(i\in I_+\)
and \(j\in I_-\), then the slice positions are \(1,0\). Formula
\eqref{eq:D2closed} gives \(D^{(2)}=0\), while \eqref{eq:Na} gives
\[
 D_0(Y_{i,1},Y_{j,0})=-\widetilde C_{ij}(2)=-B_{ij}.
\]
Thus \(\Omega(Y_{i,1},Y_{j,0})=B_{ij}\).

The Euler form \(\omega_Q\) has the same values on the \(\gamma\)-basis.
Indeed, \(\gamma_i=\alpha_i\) at a source and
\(\gamma_j=\alpha_j+\sum_{k\sim j}\alpha_k\) at a sink, so
\(\omega_Q(\gamma_i,\gamma_j)=B_{ij}\). For two sinks, the two sums over
common source neighbors occur with opposite signs and cancel. For two
sources the value is zero. Hence the two descended forms agree on a basis,
which proves the theorem.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:no-circularity}
The proof of \cref{thm:kernel} is entirely at the level of the spectral
lattice, the inverse quantum Cartan recurrence, and the bipartite
root-lattice quotient. Neither the graded-dimension theorem nor the
multiparameter realization proved later is used here. Thus the Euler
correction can be used subsequently to establish the grading and the
rank-two dimensions without circularity.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- proposition-1: body_md -->
\label{prop:torus-twist}
Under the identity on commutative Laurent monomials, the toroidal torus
over \(R'\) is the \(\kappa\)-twist of the one-parameter torus at \(v\).
Explicitly, for homogeneous elements \(x,y\) of degrees \(\alpha,\beta\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:twisted-product}
 x*y=w^{\omega_Q(\alpha,\beta)}(x*_v y).
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-1 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
For monomials the toroidal scalar in \eqref{eq:based-product} is
\(t_0^{D_0/2}w^{2D^{(2)}}\), whereas the one-parameter scalar is
\(t_0^{D_0/2}w^{D_0}\). Their quotient is
\(w^{2D^{(2)}-D_0}=w^{\omega_Q(\alpha,\beta)}\) by
\cref{thm:kernel}. Extend by bilinearity. Homogeneity is needed so that the
same scalar multiplies every monomial pair in the two elements.
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- proposition-2: body_md -->
\label{prop:characters}
After the parameter substitution and scalar extension to \(K'\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:characters}
 F_\infty(m_+)\big|_{\eqref{eq:specialization}}=F_v(m_+)
\end{equation}
as commutative-monomial expansions. Both sides are homogeneous of degree
\(\deg_Qm_+\). In particular,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:trunc-character}
 Z_{i,p}=\operatorname{tr}_Q F_v(Y_{i,p})
 \qquad((i,p)\in\widehat I_Q)
\end{equation}
after the same scalar extension.
<!-- end proposition-2 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
Every term of a character has the same \(Q\)-degree by
\cref{lem:lower,lem:mesh}.  The two summands of
\[
B_{i,p}=Y_{i,p}+Y_{i,p}A_{i,p+1}^{-1}
\]
have the same degree, and the remaining screening generators are
homogeneous Laurent variables.

Fix \(i\).  Let \(\mathscr K^{\mathrm{tor}}_i\) be the specialized
toroidal screening subalgebra and \(\mathscr K^v_i\) the corresponding
one-parameter screening subalgebra.  Both are generated by the same
homogeneous commutative-monomial expressions.  For any ordered word
\(G_1,\ldots,G_\ell\) in these homogeneous generators,
\cref{prop:torus-twist} gives
\[
G_1*\cdots*G_\ell
=
w^{c(G_1,\ldots,G_\ell)}
\bigl(G_1*_v\cdots*_vG_\ell\bigr)
\]
for an integer \(c(G_1,\ldots,G_\ell)\).  The factor on the right is a
unit of \(K'\).  Hence the identity on commutative Laurent expansions
identifies the two screening subalgebras as graded \(K'\)-vector spaces:
\[
\mathscr K^{\mathrm{tor}}_i=\mathscr K^v_i
\quad\text{inside the common Laurent-monomial vector space.}
\tag{4.12}
\]
This assertion is made separately for each \(i\); no base-change
interchange with an infinite intersection is being used.

Now let
\[
\overline F_\infty(m_+)
=
F_\infty(m_+)\big|_{\eqref{eq:specialization}}.
\]
Since \(F_\infty(m_+)\) belongs to every toroidal screening subalgebra,
(4.12) shows directly that
\[
\overline F_\infty(m_+)\in\bigcap_i\mathscr K^v_i.
\]
Its coefficient of \(m_+\) remains \(1\).  Before specialization
\(m_+\) is the only dominant exponent vector in \(F_\infty(m_+)\);
specialization can cancel existing terms but cannot create a new exponent
vector.  Thus \(m_+\) remains the unique dominant monomial of
\(\overline F_\infty(m_+)\).

The one-parameter screening intersection has the basis
\(\{F_v(m)\}\), characterized triangularly by dominant monomials
\cite{H,FH}.  This characterization survives extension of scalars to
\(K'\): if an element of the intersection has exactly one dominant
monomial \(m_+\) with coefficient \(1\), subtracting \(F_v(m_+)\) leaves
an element with no dominant monomial, hence zero.  Therefore
\[
\overline F_\infty(m_+)=F_v(m_+).
\]
Applying the same linear truncation to both sides gives
\eqref{eq:trunc-character}.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
\label{rem:basechange-intersection}
The proof deliberately avoids asserting a formal identity
\[
(\bigcap_i\mathscr K_{i,\infty})\otimes K'
=
\bigcap_i(\mathscr K_{i,\infty}\otimes K'),
\]
which would require a separate flatness argument for intersections.
Instead, it follows one already constructed element through each screening
subalgebra and then invokes the one-parameter unique-dominant
characterization.  It also uses only exponent support and screening
membership; toroidal coefficients are never interpreted as ordinary
composition multiplicities.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:graded-twist}
After extension to \(K'\), the algebra \(\mathcal G_R(Q)\) is the graded
\(\kappa\)-twist of the truncated one-parameter algebra
\(\mathcal K_v(\mathscr C_Q)\). Its positive root grading is induced by
\(\deg_Q\), and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:graded-dim}
 \dim_K\bigl(\mathcal G_R(Q)\otimes_RK\bigr)_\gamma=p(\gamma)
 \qquad(\gamma\in\mathsf L_+),
\end{equation}
where \(p(\gamma)\) is the Kostant partition number.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
The two algebras are generated by the same truncated fundamental
expressions by \cref{prop:characters}. These generators are homogeneous
and their products differ by the factors in \eqref{eq:twisted-product}.
Thus their underlying graded vector spaces over \(K'\) agree. All
generator degrees are positive roots, because \((i,p)\in\widehat I_Q\).
Hernandez--Leclerc identify the one-parameter algebra, over
\(\mathbb Q(v^{1/2})\), with the quantized positive coordinate algebra and
hence with the positive enveloping algebra after extension of scalars
\cite[Theorem 6.1]{HL}. Their identification sends the fundamental
classes to rescaled dual PBW generators of their root degree. It follows
that the dimension of a homogeneous component is \(p(\gamma)\).
The embedding in the based torus respects degree already over \(R\),
and extension from \(K\) to \(K'\) does not change vector-space
dimensions. This gives \eqref{eq:graded-dim} over \(K\).
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- proposition-3: body_md -->
\label{prop:localbasis}
The elements \(\mathsf S_{\mathbf a}\) form an \(\mathcal O\)-basis of
\(\mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q):=\mathcal G_R(Q)\otimes_R\mathcal O\). In particular, this algebra
is \(\mathcal O\)-free and its degree-\(\gamma\) component has rank
\(p(\gamma)\). Its special fiber is the one-parameter truncated
Grothendieck algebra at \(t_0\):
\begin{equation}\label{eq:specialfiberG}
 \mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q)/(u-1)\mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q)
       \simeq\mathcal K_{t_0}(\mathscr C_Q)\otimes_{\mathbb Q(t_0^{1/2})}F.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-3 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The ordinary one-parameter standard basis consists of ordered
fundamental products, normalized by quantum-torus commutation factors; see
\cite[\S5 and Theorem 6.1]{HL}. After the substitution
\(v^{1/2}=t_0^{1/2}w\), these normalization factors are monomials in
\(t_0^{1/2}\) and \(w\), hence units of \(\mathcal O'\). No assertion about an
arbitrary rational function of \(v^{1/2}\) is needed.

The character comparison \eqref{eq:characters}, initially proved over
\(K'\), identifies the same commutative-monomial expansions on the two
sides. Since the specialized toroidal generators lie in the based
\(\mathcal O'\)-torus, the corresponding one-parameter expressions do as well.
By \cref{prop:torus-twist}, every ordered homogeneous product differs from
its one-parameter counterpart by a power of \(w\), again an
\(\mathcal O'\)-unit. Consequently the elements \(\mathsf S_{\mathbf a}\)
become, after extension to \(\mathcal O'\), unit multiples of the ordinary
standard-basis elements and hence form an \(\mathcal O'\)-basis.

Consider the map from the free \(\mathcal O\)-module on these symbols to
\(\mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q)\). Its kernel and cokernel become zero after the
faithfully flat extension \(\mathcal O'\). They are consequently zero
already over \(\mathcal O\). This proves the asserted basis and ranks,
without relying on a triangular expansion in the deformed
\(F_\infty\)-basis.

Under \(u=1\), the specialized fundamental characters are the
one-parameter ones at \(t_0\). This follows either from the unique
dominant construction or by choosing \(w=1\) in the preceding character
comparison. The ordered standard products specialize to their ordinary
standard basis. The resulting surjection to the one-parameter algebra is
therefore an isomorphism of the based modules, and of algebras. This proves
\eqref{eq:specialfiberG}.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:smalldim}
If \(r\sim s\), the components of degrees
\(\alpha_r+\alpha_s\), \(2\alpha_r+\alpha_s\), and
\(\alpha_r+2\alpha_s\) have dimension two over \(K\). If
\(i\ne j\) and \(i\not\sim j\), the component of degree
\(\alpha_i+\alpha_j\) has dimension one.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Only roots supported on the indicated vertices can occur in a Kostant
partition of these degrees. For an adjacent pair, the available positive
roots are \(\alpha_r,\alpha_s,\alpha_r+\alpha_s\), giving exactly
two partitions of each listed degree. For a nonadjacent pair only the two
simple roots are available, giving one partition. Apply
\eqref{eq:graded-dim}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- proposition-4: body_md -->
\label{prop:source-base}
If \(r\in I_+\), then \(Z_r=Y_{r,1}\). If \(r\to s\) and
\(m_s=Y_{\kappa_s,p_s}\) is the highest monomial of \(Z_s\), then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:base-pair}
 (D_0,D^{(2)})(Y_{r,1},m_s)=(1,1).
\end{equation}
For distinct nonadjacent simple roots with highest monomials \(m_i,m_j\),
one has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nonadjbase}
 D_0(m_i,m_j)=D^{(2)}(m_i,m_j)=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-4 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
At a source, \(\gamma_r=\alpha_r\), so the simple-root position is
\((r,1)\). The standard initial Kirillov--Reshetikhin class with highest
monomial \(Y_{i,p}Y_{i,p+2}\cdots Y_{i,\xi_i}\) has this single
monomial as its \(Q\)-truncated character; this is the initial-character
identity in the proof of \cite[Theorem 6.1]{HL}. With \(p=\xi_r=1\)
it gives \(Z_r=Y_{r,1}\) in the one-parameter algebra, and
\cref{prop:characters} gives the same equality toroidally. No assumption
of thinness of the full fundamental module is made.

Every point of \(\widehat I_Q\) is weakly below its top height. A simple-root
point for a sink cannot have spectral coordinate \(1\), since the only
level-zero points there are the source tops and their roots are source
simple roots. Hence \(p_s<1\). The inverse-Cartan/root-pairing formula
of \cite[Proposition 3.2]{HL} gives
\[
 D_0(m_s,Y_{r,1})=(\alpha_s,\alpha_r)=-1.
\]
Skew-symmetry proves \(D_0(Y_{r,1},m_s)=1\). Since
\(\deg_QY_{r,1}=\alpha_r\), \(\deg_Qm_s=\alpha_s\), and
\(\omega_Q(\alpha_r,\alpha_s)=1\), \cref{thm:kernel} gives
\(2D^{(2)}=D_0+1=2\), proving \eqref{eq:base-pair}.

For nonadjacent simple roots, the same Hernandez--Leclerc formula gives
\(D_0(m_i,m_j)=0\) when their spectral positions differ. If the
positions agree, the kernel \eqref{eq:Na} is zero directly; no formula
requiring a strict spectral inequality is used in this case. Finally
\(\omega_Q(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)=0\), so \cref{thm:kernel} gives the
second equality in \eqref{eq:nonadjbase}.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:krylov}
Let \(\mathcal T_k\) be a based quantum torus over a field \(k\), let \(X\)
be a nonzero monomial, and let \(Z\in\mathcal T_k\) be a finite Laurent sum.
Suppose the distinct eigenvalues of \(\operatorname{Ad}_X\) on the nonzero monomial
blocks of \(Z\) are \(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_d\). Then
\[
 \dim_k\operatorname{span}_k\{Z,\operatorname{Ad}_XZ,\operatorname{Ad}_X^2Z,\ldots\}=d.
\]
If the words \(X^2Z,XZX,ZX^2\) lie in a vector space of dimension at
most two, then \(d\le2\).
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Write \(Z=\sum_{j=1}^d Z_j\), grouping its monomials by eigenvalue.
The \(Z_j\) have disjoint supports and are linearly independent. The
coefficients of \(\operatorname{Ad}_X^aZ\), for \(0\le a\le d-1\), on this
basis are the rows of the Vandermonde matrix
\((\lambda_j^a)\), whose determinant is nonzero. Higher iterates remain
in the span of the \(Z_j\), giving the first assertion.

For the second assertion, choose a nontrivial dependence
\[
 A X^2Z+B XZX+C ZX^2=0.
\]
Right multiplication in the torus by \(X^{-2}\) gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:adjointpoly}
 (A\operatorname{Ad}_X^2+B\operatorname{Ad}_X+C)Z=0.
\end{equation}
The polynomial \(AT^2+BT+C\) is nonzero. On each nonzero monomial
block it vanishes at that block's eigenvalue, so it has at least \(d\)
distinct roots. Thus \(d\le2\). No inverse of \(X\) is asserted to
belong to the original subalgebra containing the three words.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:netwall}
Every monomial occurring in \(Z\) satisfies
\begin{align}
 (D_0,D^{(2)})(X,m)
       &=(1-2\delta_r(m),\ 1-\delta_r(m)),\label{eq:netwall}\\
 \operatorname{Ad}_X(m)&=\lambda_{\delta_r(m)}m,
 \qquad \lambda_\delta=t_0^{1-2\delta}u^{2-2\delta}.
       \label{eq:lambda-delta}
\end{align}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
The highest pairing is \((1,1)\) by \eqref{eq:base-pair}. By
\cref{lem:local-AY}, every root factor other than \(A_{r,0}\) and
\(A_{r,2}\) pairs trivially with \(X\). The form on
\((X,A_{r,0})\) is \((2,1)\), and on \((X,A_{r,2})\) it is
\(-(2,1)\). Since the root factors in \eqref{eq:wallnumber} occur
inversely, their total contribution is \(-\delta_r(m)(2,1)\).
This proves \eqref{eq:netwall}, and the based-torus commutation rule gives
\eqref{eq:lambda-delta}.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:integralblocks}
Let \(Z\in\mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q)\) be a finite Laurent sum and let \(X\) be a
monomial.  Assume every monomial \(m\) in \(Z\) is an
\(\operatorname{Ad}_X\)-eigenvector and that its eigenvalue is indexed by an integer
\(\delta(m)\).  Then
\[
 Z=\sum_{\delta}Z[\delta],\qquad
 Z[\delta]=\sum_{\delta(m)=\delta}c_m\,m,
\]
is a direct decomposition in the ambient based \(\mathcal O\)-torus.  Each
\(Z[\delta]\) is defined over \(\mathcal O\), and specialization at \(u=1\) is
obtained coefficientwise:
\[
 Z[\delta]\longmapsto
 \sum_{\delta(m)=\delta}c_m(1)\,m.
\]
In particular, no denominator involving differences of eigenvalues is
introduced.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
The ambient based torus is a free \(\mathcal O\)-module on its Laurent monomial
basis.  Partitioning this basis by the integer \(\delta(m)\) therefore
gives a direct sum decomposition of the underlying \(\mathcal O\)-module.
The block \(Z[\delta]\) is simply the projection onto the corresponding
basis summand; it is not obtained by a rational polynomial in
\(\operatorname{Ad}_X\).  Hence all coefficients remain in \(\mathcal O\), and reduction
modulo \(u-1\) is coefficientwise.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:blocksurvival}
In the setting of Lemma~\ref{lem:integralblocks}, \(Z[\delta]\) vanishes
in the \(u=1\) fiber if and only if every coefficient of that block is
divisible by \(u-1\).  If all other blocks specialize to a single
\(\operatorname{Ad}_X\)-eigenvalue, then vanishing of \(Z[\delta]\) forces the whole
specialized element \(Z|_{u=1}\) to lie in that one eigenspace.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
The first assertion follows from freeness of the Laurent monomial basis
over the DVR \(\mathcal O\).  The second is immediate from the direct
coefficientwise decomposition.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:two}
For every source--sink edge in a finite simply-laced bipartite quiver,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:two}
 \operatorname{Spec}_X(Z)=\{t_0t,t_0^{-1}\}.
\end{equation}
Equivalently, \(\delta_r(m)\in\{0,1\}\) for every occurring monomial,
and the exponent pairs are exactly \((1,1)\) and \((-1,0)\).
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The spectral bound is proved over the generic field \(K\), whereas block
survival is checked over the integral local form \(\mathcal O\).  This causes no
conflict: the blocks are first defined by Laurent-monomial support over
\(\mathcal O\), then extended to \(K\) for the generic eigenvalue argument, and
finally reduced modulo \(u-1\).  Thus no eigenblock is created by scalar
extension and no projector denominator needs to be specialized.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
The three words \(X^2Z,XZX,ZX^2\) have degree
\(2\alpha_r+\alpha_s\) in \(\mathcal G_K(Q)\). Its dimension is two by
\cref{cor:smalldim}. By \cref{lem:krylov}, at most two distinct
\(\operatorname{Ad}_X\)-eigenvalues occur. The eigenvalues
\(\lambda_\delta\) in \eqref{eq:lambda-delta} are pairwise distinct,
since \(t_0,u\) are algebraically independent. Thus at most two integer
wall numbers occur.

The highest monomial has coefficient one and wall number zero. Hence the
block \(Z[0]\) is nonzero and \(\lambda_0=t_0t\) occurs. If this
were the only block over \(K\), then \(XZ=t_0tZX\). This identity is
already an identity of Laurent sums over \(\mathcal O\), so it specializes at
\(u=1\). In the one-parameter fiber, the simple-root classes correspond
to nonzero scalar multiples of adjacent Chevalley generators
\cite[\S7.1]{HL}. Those generators admit no relation of degree
\(\alpha_r+\alpha_s\); their two ordered words are independent.
The specialized equality \(XZ=t_0ZX\) is impossible. Therefore there
is a second generic block, say
\[
 Z=Z[0]+Z[d],\qquad d\ne0.
\]

By Lemma~\ref{lem:integralblocks}, these blocks are defined over the
ambient based \(\mathcal O\)-torus by direct monomial grouping; no rational
spectral projector is involved.  We do not assert that either block
belongs to \(\mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q)\).  If the second block vanished in the
special fiber, Corollary~\ref{cor:blocksurvival} would leave only the
\(\delta=0\) eigenspace and hence force the same forbidden equality
\(XZ=t_0ZX\).  Thus its specialization is nonzero.  The first block also
survives because it contains the highest monomial with coefficient one.

In the one-parameter torus, the two specialized blocks have eigenvalues
\(t_0\) and \(t_0^{1-2d}\). The ordinary adjacent Serre relation gives
\[
 (\operatorname{Ad}_X-t_0)(\operatorname{Ad}_X-t_0^{-1})Z=0.
\]
Its two terms can be separated by their disjoint monomial supports.
Since the second block is nonzero and \(d\ne0\), one must have
\(t_0^{1-2d}=t_0^{-1}\). Hence \(d=1\). Formula
\eqref{eq:netwall} gives the two asserted pairs, both of which occur.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
The proof allows coefficients of individual monomials to vanish at
\(u=1\). It requires only that the second entire block cannot vanish.
The bound on the number of generic blocks has already been proved before
specialization. This is the precise replacement for a termwise
support-preservation hypothesis in a non-thin character.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- proposition-5: body_md -->
\label{prop:forward}
One has
\begin{equation}\label{eq:forward}
 X^2Z-(t_0t+t_0^{-1})XZX+tZX^2=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end proposition-5 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
For a monomial \(m\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\in\{a,b\}\),
\[
 X^2m-(a+b)XmX+ab\,mX^2
       =(\lambda^2-(a+b)\lambda+ab)mX^2=0.
\]
Sum over the monomial expansion of \(Z\), and use \(ab=t\).
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
\label{lem:puresquares}
Let \(Z_s=P+Q\) be the two nonzero \(\operatorname{Ad}_{Z_r}\)-eigenblocks, with
\[
\operatorname{Ad}_{Z_r}(P)=aP,\qquad \operatorname{Ad}_{Z_r}(Q)=bQ,\qquad a\neq b.
\]
Then \(P^2,Q^2\neq0\) in the ambient quantum torus and are eigenvectors
with eigenvalues \(a^2,b^2\), respectively.  For the generic parameters
of this paper these eigenvalues are distinct, so the two pure-square
components of any ambient-torus relation vanish separately.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
The ambient based quantum torus is a domain, hence \(P^2,Q^2\neq0\).
Since \(\operatorname{Ad}_{Z_r}\) is an algebra automorphism,
\[
\operatorname{Ad}_{Z_r}(P^2)=a^2P^2,\qquad \operatorname{Ad}_{Z_r}(Q^2)=b^2Q^2.
\]
Here \(a=t_0t\) and \(b=t_0^{-1}\); algebraic independence of \(t_0,t\)
gives \(a^2\neq b^2\).
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:reverse}
Let \(X\) be an invertible monomial in a based torus over a field, and
let \(Z=P+Q_1\) with nonzero blocks satisfying
\(XP=aPX\), \(XQ_1=bQ_1X\). Assume \(a^2,ab,b^2\) are pairwise
distinct and \(Z^2X,ZXZ,XZ^2\) are linearly dependent. If the ambient
torus is a domain, their unique normalized relation is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reverse-general}
 Z^2X-(a^{-1}+b^{-1})ZXZ+(ab)^{-1}XZ^2=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Take an actual nonzero relation
\begin{equation}\label{eq:actual-reverse}
 A Z^2X+B ZXZ+C XZ^2=0.
\end{equation}
The pure \(P^2\), mixed \(PQ_1,Q_1P\), and pure \(Q_1^2\)
contributions have respective \(\operatorname{Ad}_X\)-eigenvalues
\(a^2,ab,b^2\). Multiplication by \(X\) does not change them. Thus the
three groups separate; in particular, neither mixed group can contaminate
a pure group. With \(X\) moved to the right, the pure contributions are
\[
 \begin{array}{c|ccc}
 &Z^2X&ZXZ&XZ^2\\ \hline
 P^2&P^2X&aP^2X&a^2P^2X\\
 Q_1^2&Q_1^2X&bQ_1^2X&b^2Q_1^2X.
 \end{array}
\]
Because the torus is a domain these pure factors are nonzero. Hence
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reverse-coeff}
 A+Ba+Ca^2=0,\qquad A+Bb+Cb^2=0.
\end{equation}
If \(A=0\), division by \(a,b\) and subtraction give \(C=0\), then
\(B=0\), a contradiction. Normalize \(A=1\). The equations imply
\[
 B=-C(a+b),\qquad 1-Cab=0,
\]
so \(C=(ab)^{-1}\) and \(B=-(a^{-1}+b^{-1})\).
The coefficients of the actual relation \eqref{eq:actual-reverse} are
therefore uniquely fixed, proving \eqref{eq:reverse-general}. No
commutation relation between \(P\) and \(Q_1\) was assumed: the mixed
part satisfies the result because it was part of an existing relation.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:reverse}
For a source--sink edge \(r\to s\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:reverse}
 Z_s^2Z_r-(t_0+t_0^{-1}t^{-1})Z_sZ_rZ_s+t^{-1}Z_rZ_s^2=0.
\end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
The three words have degree \(\alpha_r+2\alpha_s\) and are linearly
dependent by \cref{cor:smalldim}. Both blocks are nonzero by
\cref{thm:two}. Moreover,
\[
 a^2=t_0^2t^2,\qquad ab=t,\qquad b^2=t_0^{-2}
\]
are pairwise distinct over \(K\). Apply \cref{lem:reverse}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- lemma-11: body_md -->
\label{lem:highratio}
Suppose \(Z_iZ_j=cZ_jZ_i\) for a scalar \(c\) and let \(m_i,m_j\)
be the highest monomials. Then
\[
 c=t_0^{D_0(m_i,m_j)}t^{D^{(2)}(m_i,m_j)}.
\]
For nonadjacent distinct simple roots, \(Z_iZ_j=Z_jZ_i\).
<!-- end lemma-11 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
The highest monomial of each factor has coefficient one. A term obtained
by lowering either factor cannot produce \(m_im_j\): the ratio from
that highest product would be a product of inverse root monomials with
nonnegative exponents. It is nontrivial by \cref{lem:Aindependent},
or simply by its strictly negative ordinary-weight height. Thus the
coefficient of \(m_im_j\) comes only from the two highest terms. Their
coefficients in the two product orders are inverse based-torus factors.
Their ratio is the stated scalar.

For nonadjacent vertices the two products are nonzero and lie in the
one-dimensional component of degree \(\alpha_i+\alpha_j\), so such
an equality exists. By \eqref{eq:nonadjbase}, its scalar is \(1\).
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- proposition-6: body_md -->
\label{prop:hprcompat}
For an oriented adjacent edge \(i\to j\), put
\[
q_{ii}=q_{jj}=t_0^2t,\qquad
q_{ij}=t_0^{-1},\qquad q_{ji}=t_0^{-1}t^{-1}.
\]
Then
\[
q_{ij}q_{ji}=q_{ii}^{-1}=q_{ii}^{a_{ij}},
\]
and the standard simply-laced Cartan-type Serre coefficients are
\[
(1+q_{ii})q_{ij}=t_0^{-1}+t_0t,\qquad
q_{ii}q_{ij}^2=t,
\]
and
\[
(1+q_{jj})q_{ji}=t_0+t_0^{-1}t^{-1},\qquad
q_{jj}q_{ji}^2=t^{-1}.
\]
Thus the forward and reverse toroidal Serre relations use the same
ordered matrix \(\mathbf q\), with no interchange of \(q_{ij}\) and
\(q_{ji}\).
<!-- end proposition-6 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
All four identities follow by direct substitution.  The first is
\[
t_0^{-1}(t_0^{-1}t^{-1})
=t_0^{-2}t^{-1}
=(t_0^2t)^{-1},
\]
and the remaining identities are immediate expansions.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
If \(a_{ij}=0\), the Euler-correction identity gives zero toroidal
exponent on nonadjacent simple roots.  Hence
\[
q_{ij}=q_{ji}=1,
\]
so the nonadjacent Cartan relation is ordinary commutation.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- proposition-7: body_md -->
\label{prop:Cartan-rel}
The parameters \eqref{eq:qcompact} satisfy the Cartan constraint, and
the assignment \(E_i\mapsto Z_i\) satisfies all relations
\eqref{eq:HPRzero}--\eqref{eq:HPRserre}.
<!-- end proposition-7 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
Skewness of \(\omega_Q\) gives
\(q_{ij}q_{ji}=v^{2c_{ij}}=q_{ii}^{c_{ij}}\).
On an edge \(r\to s\),
\begin{align*}
 (1+q_{rr})q_{rs}&=t_0^{-1}+t_0t,&
 q_{rr}q_{rs}^2&=t,\\
 (1+q_{ss})q_{sr}&=t_0+t_0^{-1}t^{-1},&
 q_{ss}q_{sr}^2&=t^{-1}.
\end{align*}
The claims follow from \cref{prop:forward,cor:reverse,lem:highratio}.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- lemma-12: body_md -->
\label{lem:cocycle}
Twisting the homogeneous product of the one-parameter positive part by
\(x\star y=\sigma(|x|,|y|)xy\) changes its parameters to
\(q_{ij}=\bar q_{ij}\sigma_{ij}/\sigma_{ji}\), where
\(\sigma_{ij}=\sigma(\alpha_i,\alpha_j)\).
<!-- end lemma-12 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
For an adjacent pair, bicharacter multiplicativity gives
\begin{align*}
 E_i\star E_i\star E_j&=\sigma_{ii}\sigma_{ij}^2E_i^2E_j,\\
 E_i\star E_j\star E_i&=\sigma_{ii}\sigma_{ij}\sigma_{ji}E_iE_jE_i,\\
 E_j\star E_i\star E_i&=\sigma_{ii}\sigma_{ji}^2E_jE_i^2.
\end{align*}
Multiply the ordinary Serre relation by \(\sigma_{ii}\sigma_{ij}^2\)
and rewrite the products. Its middle coefficient becomes
\((1+\bar q_{ii})\bar q_{ij}\sigma_{ij}/\sigma_{ji}\), and its
last coefficient becomes
\(\bar q_{ii}\bar q_{ij}^2(\sigma_{ij}/\sigma_{ji})^2\).
This is \eqref{eq:HPRserre} with the stated parameter. The nonadjacent
two-term relation transforms by the same ratio. Applying the inverse twist
recovers the original relations; hence this calculation identifies the
presentations, not merely a quotient of one presentation.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- proposition-8: body_md -->
\label{prop:PBW}
There is an \(\mathcal O\)-algebra \(U_{\mathbf q,\mathcal O}^+\) with a free
ordered PBW \(\mathcal O\)-basis, generic fiber \(U_{\mathbf q}^+\), and
special fiber \(U_{t_0}^+(\mathfrak g)\).
<!-- end proposition-8 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
Take a standard ordered PBW basis of the one-parameter positive part
with parameter \(v=t_0u\).  We use the local lattice spanned by these
ordered PBW vectors over \(\mathcal O\).  The structure constants needed for
multiplication lie in the localization because their denominators are the
standard quantum normalizing factors evaluated at the generic parameter
\(v\); at \(u=1\) these specialize to nonzero rational functions of the
transcendental variable \(t_0\).  Hence the required normalizing factors
are \(\mathcal O\)-units.  We do not claim that an arbitrary nonzero rational
function of \(v\) is a unit at the special fiber.

The ordinary PBW theorem gives freeness of this local lattice.  The
multiparameter cocycle/shuffle framework is used only to identify the
twisted generic multiplication with the Cartan-type presentation
\cite{HPR}.

Twist the multiplication by \eqref{eq:sigma}. All twist values are
\(\mathcal O\)-units, so the underlying free module is unchanged. By
\cref{lem:cocycle} and its inverse-twist argument, the generic fiber is
the Cartan-type positive part with parameters \(\mathbf q\). At
\(u=1\), the cocycle is identically one and \(v=t_0\), proving the
special-fiber assertion. This constructs the local form; it is not an
assertion that a particular integral form over all of \(R\) was already
proved in \cite{HPR}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- lemma-13: body_md -->
\label{lem:simplefiber}
Under the Hernandez--Leclerc identification of the fiber
\eqref{eq:specialfiberG} with \(U_{t_0}^+\),
\[
 \overline Z_i\longmapsto c_iE_i,\qquad c_i\in F^\times.
\]
The assignment \(E_i\mapsto c_iE_i\) is an automorphism.
<!-- end lemma-13 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The highest monomial of \(Z_i\) has coefficient one, so its reduction
is nonzero. The fundamental simple-root class has degree \(\alpha_i\)
in the graded identification of \cite[Theorem 6.1 and \S7.1]{HL}.
The \(\alpha_i\)-component of the positive part is one-dimensional.
Hence its image is a nonzero scalar multiple of \(E_i\). Every
presentation relation is root-homogeneous, so scaling the generators by
the nonzero \(c_i\) preserves all relations and has the inverse scaling.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- lemma-14: body_md -->
\label{lem:kerneldescent}
The local target \(\mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q)\) is torsion-free over the DVR \(\mathcal O\).
If the generic homomorphism
\[
\Phi_K:U_{\mathbf q,\mathcal O}^+\otimes_{\mathcal O}K
\longrightarrow
\mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q)\otimes_{\mathcal O}K
\]
has nonzero kernel, then \(\Phi_{\mathcal O}\) has a nonzero kernel element
whose reduction modulo \(u-1\) is nonzero.
<!-- end lemma-14 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
The local standard basis established earlier makes
\(\mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q)\) a free, hence torsion-free, \(\mathcal O\)-module.
Let \(0\ne x_K\in\ker\Phi_K\).  Clearing the finitely many denominators
of its PBW coefficients gives \(0\ne x\in U_{\mathbf q,\mathcal O}^+\) whose
image becomes zero after localization.  Therefore some nonzero
\(a\in\mathcal O\) satisfies
\[
a\,\Phi_{\mathcal O}(x)=0.
\]
Torsion-freeness of the target implies \(\Phi_{\mathcal O}(x)=0\).

Write
\[
x=\sum_{\mathbf a}f_{\mathbf a}(u)E^{\mathbf a}
\]
in the free PBW basis and let
\[
d=\min_{f_{\mathbf a}\ne0}\operatorname{ord}_{u-1}f_{\mathbf a}.
\]
Then \(x=(u-1)^dy\) for a PBW-lattice element \(y\), and at least one
coefficient of \(y\) is a unit.  Since
\[
0=\Phi_{\mathcal O}(x)=(u-1)^d\Phi_{\mathcal O}(y)
\]
and the target is torsion-free, \(\Phi_{\mathcal O}(y)=0\).  The reduction of
\(y\) modulo \(u-1\) is nonzero by construction.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:main}
For every finite simply-laced bipartite quiver \(Q\),
\begin{equation}\label{eq:mainiso}
 \Phi:U_{\mathbf q}^+(\mathfrak g)\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }
              \mathcal G_R(Q)\otimes_RK,\qquad E_i\longmapsto Z_i.
\end{equation}
The parameters are given by \eqref{eq:intro-q}. Thus the isomorphism is
over \(K\), without the auxiliary scalar extension \(K'\).
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
The equality of graded dimensions used at the end of
Theorem~\ref{thm:main} was established before the local spectral theorem,
via the Euler-correction identity, the graded torus twist, character
comparison, and the Hernandez--Leclerc one-parameter PBW basis.  It does
not use the multiparameter realization.  Thus injectivity plus equal
graded dimensions is a genuine final step rather than a restatement of
the theorem being proved.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
By \cref{prop:Cartan-rel,prop:PBW}, the assignment defines an
\(\mathcal O\)-homomorphism
\[
 \Phi_{\mathcal O}:U_{\mathbf q,\mathcal O}^+\longrightarrow\mathcal G_{\mathcal O}(Q)
\]
and hence the desired generic homomorphism. Its special fiber is an
isomorphism by \cref{prop:localbasis,lem:simplefiber}.

If the generic kernel were nonzero, Lemma~\ref{lem:kerneldescent}
would produce a nonzero element of the local kernel with nonzero reduction
modulo \(u-1\).  But the special fiber of the source is
\(U_{t_0}^+(\mathfrak g)\), the special fiber of the target is the
Hernandez--Leclerc algebra, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:simplefiber} the induced
map is the diagonal automorphism
\[
E_i\longmapsto c_iE_i,\qquad c_i\in F^\times.
\]
Its kernel is zero, a contradiction.  Hence \(\Phi\) is injective.

The map preserves \(\mathsf L_+\)-degrees. In every degree its source has
PBW dimension \(p(\gamma)\), while its target has the same dimension
by \cref{thm:graded-twist}. An injective map between these two finite
dimensional spaces is surjective. Therefore \(\Phi\) is an
isomorphism in every degree and proves \eqref{eq:mainiso}.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- proposition-9: body_md -->
\label{prop:cluster}
If
\[
 \widetilde B^T\Lambda_0=(2I_m\mid0),\qquad G\widetilde B=0,
\]
then the second toroidal commutation matrix is
\begin{equation}\label{eq:Lambda2}
 \Lambda_2=\frac12\left(\Lambda_0+G^TW_QG\right),
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:twocompat}
 \widetilde B^T\Lambda_2=(I_m\mid0).
\end{equation}
When \(\Lambda_2\) is integral, these are two compatible skew forms
for a toroidal seed with parameters \(t_0,t\).
<!-- end proposition-9 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
The quasi-commutation factor of two homogeneous seed variables in the
moving one-parameter torus is \(v^{\Lambda_0(i,j)}\). Twisting by
\(\kappa\) changes it by
\(\kappa(g_i,g_j)/\kappa(g_j,g_i)=u^{\omega_Q(g_i,g_j)}\).
Thus the factor is
\[
 t_0^{\Lambda_0(i,j)}u^{\Lambda_0(i,j)+\omega_Q(g_i,g_j)}
 =t_0^{\Lambda_0(i,j)}t^{\Lambda_2(i,j)},
\]
proving \eqref{eq:Lambda2}. Matrix multiplication gives
\[
 \widetilde B^TG^TW_QG=(G\widetilde B)^TW_QG=0.
\]
Now \eqref{eq:twocompat} follows by taking one half of the first
compatibility identity. Skewness is clear. For a seed realized in the
original integral two-parameter based torus the integrality is already
part of its exponent data; for abstract homogeneous seed data it is an
explicit hypothesis, not an automatic consequence of homogeneity alone.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- proposition-10: body_md -->
\label{prop:mutation}
Under homogeneous seed mutation, \eqref{eq:Lambda2} transforms by the
usual skew-form mutation. In particular, the two compatible forms remain
compatible along the mutation pattern.
<!-- end proposition-10 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
Use the standard mutation matrix \(E\) on the lattice of seed exponents.
It is the identity on columns other than the mutated column \(k\), with
\[
 E e_k=-e_k+\sum_i[-b_{ik}]_+e_i.
\]
The degree of the new cluster variable is the common degree of the two
exchange terms minus \(g_k\); hence \(G'=GE\). The ordinary skew
form transforms as \(\Lambda_0'=E^T\Lambda_0E\). Therefore
\begin{align*}
 \Lambda_2'&=\tfrac12\bigl(\Lambda_0'+(G')^TW_QG'\bigr)\\
 &=E^T\tfrac12\bigl(\Lambda_0+G^TW_QG\bigr)E
   =E^T\Lambda_2E.
\end{align*}
The standard compatible-pair mutation identity of \cite{BZ} applies to
each form, or equivalently one may use \cite[Proposition 2.3]{FH}.
The mutated exchange relation remains homogeneous, so \(G'\widetilde
B'=0\) as required for the next step.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
